content.title: About
content.content: Figs (Ficus carica) are soft, sweet, teardrop-shaped fruits with thin skin, a jammy, honeyed pulp, and many tiny crunchy seeds, native to the Middle East and Mediterranean. They range from green and yellow to purple and brown. Figs are eaten fresh or dried and used in salads, desserts, baking, and jams.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: A fig is not a true fruit in the usual sense but an inverted flower cluster, called a syconium, with the tiny flowers inside.
Figs are among the oldest cultivated fruit trees, grown for thousands of years.
Fresh figs are very delicate and perishable, which is why dried figs are so common.
The crunchy bits inside are the fig's tiny seeds, which are edible.
Figs are an important fruit in Central Asian, Middle Eastern, and Mediterranean cuisines.

items.title: Provides dietary fiber
items.content: Figs are a good source of fiber, which supports digestion and regularity.

items.title: Provides potassium and calcium
items.content: These minerals support normal blood pressure and bones.

items.title: Provides vitamin K and copper
items.content: These nutrients support blood clotting and metabolism.

items.title: Contains polyphenols
items.content: Figs contain plant compounds with antioxidant properties, especially in dark varieties.

items.title: Natural sweetness
items.content: Figs provide natural sweetness along with fiber.

items.title: Natural sugars and calories
items.content: Figs, especially dried figs, are high in natural sugars and calories for their weight.

items.title: Digestive effects
items.content: Eating a lot of figs may cause loose stools or bloating because of fiber and sorbitol.

items.title: Allergic reactions and latex
items.content: Some people, especially those with latex or birch pollen allergy, may react to figs, and the sap can irritate the skin.

items.title: Possible medication interactions
items.content: Figs contain vitamin K. People taking blood thinners should consult a healthcare professional about keeping their intake consistent.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Fresh figs can be eaten whole or halved, with cheese and nuts, in salads, roasted, or baked into tarts and cakes. Dried figs can be eaten as a snack, chopped into oatmeal, yogurt, and baking, or simmered into compotes. Use small portions of dried figs.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Fresh figs are very perishable. Store them in the refrigerator in a single layer and eat them within two to three days. Dried figs keep for several months in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. Discard figs that are moldy or smell fermented.

content.title: About
content.content: Pickled fruit consists of fresh fruit that has been preserved in a brine made of vinegar, sugar, and spices. The pickling process retains part of the fruit’s natural flavor while adding a tangy‑sweet note and extending shelf life.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pickled fruit is popular in Mediterranean, Asian, and Eastern European cuisines.
Common fruits for pickling include apples, pears, peaches, pineapple, and mango.
Spices such as cinnamon, clove, ginger, and mustard seeds are often added to the brine for extra aroma.
Pickling helps preserve vitamin C and some polyphenols, although a portion is lost due to acidity.
In some cultures, pickled fruit is served as a side dish with meat.

items.title: Rich in vitamins
items.content: Pickled fruit retains vitamin C, vitamin A, and several B‑vitamins that support immunity and vision.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Phytochemicals such as polyphenols help combat free radicals.

items.title: Supports gut microbiota
items.content: A small amount of probiotic bacteria may survive the pickling process, benefiting gut health.

items.title: Improves iron absorption
items.content: The acidic environment enhances the absorption of non‑heme iron from plant foods.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Brine often contains a lot of sugar, which can be problematic for people with diabetes or those watching their weight.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Vinegar can irritate the stomach in individuals with gastritis or ulcer disease.

items.title: Sodium levels
items.content: Salt in the brine raises sodium intake, a concern for hypertension.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to specific fruits or added spices.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pickled fruit can be enjoyed as a snack, added to salads, desserts, yogurts, smoothies, or used as a garnish for meat dishes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the jar of pickled fruit in the refrigerator at 2‑4 °C. Once opened, consume within 2‑3 weeks. Discard if mold appears or the smell changes.

content.title: About
content.content: A milk shake is a beverage made from milk, ice cream or frozen yogurt, and various flavorings. In a home recipe you can use fresh fruit, berries, nuts, spices and sweeteners to create a wide range of flavors other than the classic chocolate.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The milk shake originated in the United States in the early 20th century and quickly became popular in diners and restaurants.
In Russia the drink is often called “milk frappe,” especially when served over ice.
There are more than 100 flavor variations, including vanilla, strawberry, banana, mango, caramel and nutty.
A homemade shake lets you control sugar levels and add nutritious ingredients such as chia seeds or protein powder.
The traditional preparation method is blending, but a shaker can be used for a lighter texture.

items.title: Calcium source
items.content: Milk, the main ingredient, is rich in calcium, which supports bone and tooth health.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Adding yogurt, ice cream or protein powder boosts the protein content, aiding muscle recovery.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Milk provides vitamin B2 (riboflavin) and B12, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Probiotics
items.content: Using kefir or live‑culture yogurt can contribute beneficial bacteria for gut health.

items.title: Antioxidants from fruit
items.content: Berries, mango, kiwi and other fruits add vitamin C and polyphenols that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: People with lactose intolerance should use lactose‑free milk or plant‑based alternatives.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Store‑bought ice cream and added sweeteners can raise calories and blood sugar levels.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Casein and whey proteins may trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Shakes made with ice cream and cream can be very calorie‑rich; watch portion size if weight management is a goal.

content.title: How to Make
content.content: Combine 200 ml of milk (or a plant‑based alternative), 2 tablespoons of ice cream or yogurt, your chosen flavoring (fruit, nuts, spices) and a sweetener to taste in a blender. Blend until smooth and creamy; add ice if a thicker texture is desired. Serve immediately, garnished with berries, sprinkles or mint.

content.title: Storage
content.content: A milk shake is best enjoyed right away. If you need to store it, keep it in a sealed container in the refrigerator for no more than 24 hours; give it a quick stir before serving as ingredients may separate.

content.title: About
content.content: Pie with banana cream is a dessert consisting of a tender crust, a layer of sweet banana cream, and often topped with glaze or a sprinkle. The banana cream is made from ripe bananas, cream cheese, sugar, and sometimes heavy cream, giving it a smooth, aromatic texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Banana cream is a popular filling in American and European pastries, especially during the summer season.
Traditional recipes use fully ripe bananas, which reduces the need for added sugar.
The pie can be made with various crusts: shortcrust, yeasted, or gluten‑free.
Bananas are one of the most nutrient‑dense fruits, high in potassium and vitamin B6.
In some countries the pie is served with a scoop of vanilla ice cream.

items.title: Rich in potassium
items.content: Bananas provide a high amount of potassium, which supports normal heart and muscle function.

items.title: Source of vitamin B6
items.content: Vitamin B6 is involved in protein metabolism and neurotransmitter synthesis.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber in bananas promotes healthy digestion.

items.title: Antioxidant content
items.content: Bananas contain vitamin C and other antioxidants that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Energy boost
items.content: Combined carbohydrates from the crust and natural fruit sugars provide a quick source of energy.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: The cream is often made with cream cheese or heavy cream, which can trigger reactions in people with lactose intolerance or dairy allergy.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: The pie can be sweet, so individuals monitoring blood glucose should watch portion size.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Both crust and cream make the dessert calorie‑rich; moderate consumption is advised for weight management.

items.title: Gluten content
items.content: Traditional crust contains gluten, which may be problematic for those with celiac disease.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the pie at room temperature, sliced into portions. It pairs well with vanilla ice cream, whipped cream, or a berry sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the pie refrigerated, covered with plastic wrap, for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze in an airtight container for up to 2 months. Allow it to come to room temperature briefly before serving.

white-pizza-cheese-with-meat-thin-crust.title: White Pizza with Cheese and Meat, Thin Crust

content.title: About
content.content: White pizza with cheese and meat on a thin crust is a classic Italian pizza that skips the tomato sauce. Instead, a creamy base made from ricotta or mozzarella cheese is spread, topped with assorted meats (ham, sausage, bacon) and grated cheese. The thin crust keeps the dish light and crisp.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: White pizza ("pizza bianca") originated in Naples as an alternative to tomato‑based pies.
The creamy sauce is often a blend of heavy cream, ricotta, and garlic, giving a delicate flavor.
Thin crust is made from high‑grade flour, water, yeast, and a small amount of olive oil.
Typical meat toppings include ham, salami, prosciutto, and sometimes chicken.
In some regions, spinach or artichokes are added to the white pizza for extra texture.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Meat and cheese provide high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Calcium and vitamin D
items.content: Cheese supplies calcium, supporting bone and dental health.

items.title: Lower carbohydrate crust
items.content: A thin crust contains fewer carbs than a traditional thick crust, which can help blood‑sugar control.

items.title: Healthy fats
items.content: Olive oil in the dough and the creamy sauce contain monounsaturated fats beneficial for the heart.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Meat and cheese are good sources of B6 and B12, important for nervous system function and red blood cell formation.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: The creamy sauce and cheese make the pizza calorie‑dense; portion control is advised.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Large amounts of cheese and meat can increase saturated fat intake, which may be a concern for heart disease.

items.title: Sodium
items.content: Processed meats often contain a lot of salt, potentially raising blood pressure.

items.title: Dairy allergy or lactose intolerance
items.content: People with dairy sensitivities should choose lactose‑free or dairy‑free cheese alternatives.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Traditional crust contains gluten; a gluten‑free base is needed for those with celiac disease.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the pizza hot, cut into slices, and optionally garnish with fresh arugula or basil for brightness. A sprinkle of grated Parmesan or a dash of freshly ground black pepper adds extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. Reheat in an oven or grill to restore the crisp crust.
